title: States furious at stamp duty hit
full_text:
Tasmania and Queensland have taken aim at Jim Chalmers over the impact of the federal budget on their revenues, as the federal Coalition claims the states will be hit by an $8bn drop in stamp duty collections.
Tasmanian Treasurer Eric Abetz said the Liberal state government was monitoring the impact that these “damaging federal tax changes are having here”.
“It is on federal Labor to ensure Tasmanians are not left worse off,” Mr Abetz said.
Queensland Treasurer David Janetzki said: “Queenslanders are now also paying the price for Jim Chalmers’ budget decisions.” NSW Treasurer Daniel Mookhey said the state had already downgraded stamp duty revenue “after the RBA raised interest rates three times earlier this year”.
“We’ll continue to watch the market closely and if any adjustments to revenue estimates are needed, they’ll be reflected in the half-yearly review,” he said.
The Coalition analysis provided to The Australian predicted stamp duty revenues could fall $8bn below forecasts in 2026-27, with NSW leading the way with a $2.8bn hit.
Under a scenario where values fall by 10 per cent and property sales drop by 20 per cent, stamp duty revenues would decline by $2.1bn in Victoria, $1.7bn in Queensland and $950m in Western Australia.
The Coalition’s estimate would see stamp duty collections drops by 28 per cent compared to 2025-26.
The major banks are expecting home price falls of between 7 per cent and 10.6 per cent, while HSBC is estimating a 13 per cent decline in values nationally.
Dr Chalmers last week admitted the budget tax changes were one of the reasons capital city home prices had declined by 3.7 per cent in the three months to September. “It’s a factor but not the only factor,” he said.
The Reserve Bank and industry groups are also warning the budget tax hikes will impact new housing construction.
Angus Taylor said Labor was overseeing a “trifecta of failure on housing with fewer homes, higher rents and confidence in the housing market smashed”.
“They have managed to turn a cost-of-living crisis into a housing crisis, and now state budgets are being dragged into the mess as well,” the Opposition Leader said.
“When home buyers disappear, transactions dry up and house prices fall, state governments lose billions in stamp duty. That is the real-world consequence of getting economic policy wrong. Australians are already paying the price through higher mortgages, higher rents and falling confidence. Now taxpayers face another bill as state revenues are smashed.” In question time on Thursday, the Treasurer said the number of mortgage holders falling into negative equity was “very limited”.
“It affects less than 1 per cent of all borrowers in the view of the RBA,” Dr Chalmers said.
“Just this week the (Commonwealth Bank’s) executive general manager of home buying said that they had fewer customers in negative equity now than at the at the same time last year.” He said the number of mortgage holders in negative equity was “twice as high” in 2019 when the Coalition was in government.
“If they were being upfront, they would acknowledge, as all the experts, there are a number of factors playing out in the housing market,” he said.
With budget tax changes contributing to national house price declines, Reserve Bank of Australia chief economist Sarah Hunter last week said the impact on supply would be felt later in the year. “(Interest rate rises, tax changes, and the war in the Middle East are) going to have an impact on new dwelling supply in the future, which is, as I said, that’s why we’ve got a new dwelling supply profile that has activity dropping down, at the end of the forecast horizon,” she said.
